content.p: At dawn on Saturday 23 March 2019, armed men in the traditional dress of Dogon hunters entered Ogossagou, a village of Fulani herders in the Mopti region of central Mali, and killed its inhabitants where they found them. The United Nations mission in the country, MINUSMA, counted at least 157 dead. Rights groups and some press reports spoke of about 160. NBC News described it as among the worst episodes of bloodshed in Mali's ethnic conflict.

None of the reporting consulted records a conviction for it. The militia widely blamed, Dan Na Ambassagou, denied involvement. Eleven months later armed men returned to the same village and killed dozens more, in an attack that Human Rights Watch said the Malian army and the UN might have prevented.
content.h2: A region at war with itself
content.p: Ogossagou lies a short distance south of the town of Bankass, close to the border with Burkina Faso. Human Rights Watch put the village at about 15 kilometres from Bankass and at more than a thousand inhabitants, with Fulani (also called Peuhl) and Dogon families living in separate neighbourhoods about 300 metres apart. Fulani herders and Dogon farmers had long argued over grazing land and water. Middle East Eye quoted analysts who said such violence had historically been rare until armed groups inspired by extremist ideology rose in the region from 2015.

Among those groups was the Macina Liberation Front, led by the preacher Amadou Koufa, responsible for attacks on government and army positions. It recruited mostly from Fulani communities, and it later became part of the al-Qaeda-aligned coalition JNIM. As the state pulled back, Dogon village defence groups formed. FIDH said such militias had committed attacks on other communities since 2016. Dan Na Ambassagou, "Hunters who trust in God", came together in December 2016, according to the research group ACLED, after jihadists believed to be Fulani killed the leader of the Dogon hunters' fraternity. Its military wing was led by Youssouf Toloba. ACLED said estimates of its strength ran from several hundred to 5,000.

The cost to civilians was already heavy. The Defense Post cited UN figures of 500 civilians killed in 2018 alone, and the previous January, 37 people died in Koulogon, another Fulani village, and Dogon hunters were blamed. Ibrahim Yahaya of the International Crisis Group told Middle East Eye that Dogon militias had come to see Fulani as "being in bed with the jihadists" and had struck their villages without distinction. The Fulani, who number almost three million in Mali according to the same article, are increasingly the focus of the violence, partly because they are seen as tied to the armed jihadist groups, and one Fulani leader called what was happening a genocide. The government denied claims that it ignored or encouraged such attacks.

The trigger, according to several accounts, came days earlier. An al-Qaeda affiliate attacked an army post in central Mali and killed at least 23 soldiers. African Arguments described the Ogossagou attack as an apparent reprisal for that assault.

MINUSMA's investigators, who were in the area between 25 and 29 March, concluded that at least 100 armed dozo hunters took part, accompanied by about a dozen men in military clothing and others in civilian clothes. The attack began at about 5 a.m. with a confrontation between the hunters and armed Fulani men in the village, who the mission said were candidates for a voluntary disarmament programme and had set up a self-defence group. The dozos then moved through the Fulani part of the village, MINUSMA said, killing men, women and children without distinction. Most victims were shot.

The mission recorded at least 157 dead, among them at least 12 members of the self-defence group, and 65 wounded by gunfire, knives or other violence. At the hospital in Sevare, 43 patients were treated, 17 of them children. Its team found three mass graves, two with at least 40 bodies each and one with at least 70. AMDH and FIDH reported that more than 450 homes were burned and livestock slaughtered.

The first counts were lower and varied by who gave them. A local mayor said 115 dead, the governor of the Bankass district gave a provisional 115, and the mayor of Bankass told Reuters that gendarmes had recovered 134 bodies. The Defense Post, reporting that day, said that the victims had been shot or hacked with machetes, according to a security source, and that witnesses told AFP the hunters had burned nearly all the huts. A French analyst of Fulani societies told Middle East Eye that victims had been burned alive and throats cut. The UN human rights office spokeswoman, Ravina Shamdasani, called the attacks "horrific".
A neighbouring Fulani hamlet, Welingara, was also attacked, according to the Bankass mayor. MINUSMA said that a Dogon village was struck the same night and at least four people died there.

The governor of the Bankass district said survivors had accused traditional hunters. Malian officials said they suspected Dan Na Ambassagou. The group denied its members were involved and rejected the government's decision to dissolve it, according to NBC News and Al Jazeera. FIDH and AMDH, for their part, attributed the massacre to the militia and said it followed a series of massacres in the Koro district documented in their own report of November 2018.

The UN mission was careful in its legal language. It called the attack "planned, organized and coordinated" and part of a pattern: more than 37 incidents in the Bankass district since November 2018, with at least 115 deaths, had been attributed to traditional hunters' groups. The abuses "could be described as crimes against humanity", it said, if it were shown that the attack formed part of a systematic or generalized attack on civilians. International Criminal Court prosecutor Fatou Bensouda said that the crimes could fall within the court's jurisdiction and that a delegation would be sent to Mali.
content.h2: Dismissals, a dissolved militia and a fallen government
content.p: The massacre struck while a delegation of the UN Security Council was visiting the Sahel. On 24 March the government announced that it had replaced senior military officers, among them the chief of the armed forces' general staff and the army chief of staff, according to FIDH, and also dissolved Dan Na Ambassagou, saying the association had departed from its original aims despite repeated warnings. The group had said on 20 March that it would resume patrols because of attacks by "armed bandits dressed in uniform". African Arguments said the dismissed officers had tolerated and promoted coordination between security forces and militias like it.

FIDH pointed out that dissolving the militia was not enough on its own. It called for impartial investigations, prosecutions of those who ordered and carried out the killings, and the disarming of all militias in the centre and north. Four weeks later, on 18 April, Prime Minister Maiga and his government resigned. The president's office gave no reason. Legislators had been discussing a no-confidence motion over the massacre and over the failure to disarm armed groups. Al Jazeera reported that five people suspected of taking part had been detained, but the group many believed organised the attack had not been disarmed despite pledges from both the president and the prime minister.

After the 2019 killings a post of about 40 soldiers was set up in Ogossagou, and Fulani families from other attacked villages gathered there for safety. Villagers told Human Rights Watch that President Ibrahim Boubacar Keita had come to offer condolences and promised the troops would stay.

On the afternoon of 13 February 2020, villagers watched the soldiers pack up and leave without explanation. Residents and Fulani leaders in Bamako said they phoned ministers and MINUSMA to warn of an attack. Within hours, villagers said, they saw armed men gather in the Dogon neighbourhood. A UN convoy passed through an hour before the attack but left after being apparently misdirected, witnesses said. Shortly after 5 a.m. on 14 February the shooting started, according to Human Rights Watch. Armed Dogon men chased people into the bush; this time, one villager said, most were killed there rather than in their houses. The killing ended about three hours later when Malian troops and UN peacekeepers arrived. One attacker was arrested.

The counts differ. Al Jazeera, on the day, reported at least 21 dead or missing, with Fulani association Tabital Pulaaku putting it at a minimum of 22. Human Rights Watch, after interviews with 18 people, estimated 36 killed, including four children, and 19 missing. The organisation said about 700 animals were looted. Witnesses gave it the names of 20 Dogon men they said they recognised, including some who allegedly took part in 2019. Two Malian officials told HRW that a local Dan Na Ambassagou commander was suspected of planning the attack and distributing ammunition, and that as far as HRW could determine he had not been questioned. Dan Na Ambassagou issued a statement on 15 February denying responsibility. Two Dogon men said unidentified assailants were responsible and pointed to recent killings and cattle theft by armed Fulani men.

Two ministries told the rights group that a "tactical error" had caused the withdrawal and that disciplinary measures had been taken. "If those who killed in 2019 were put in jail, this second attack wouldn't have happened," a witness told HRW.

The violence did not stop with Ogossagou. ACLED recorded campaigns by JNIM against Dan Na Ambassagou from late 2019, including a March 2020 battle at Borko village in which over 100 militiamen were reported killed. It said relations between the militia and the state remained ambiguous: at times they patrolled together, at times the army fought the group. When Malian forces and the Wagner Group resumed operations in the region in late 2021, cooperation with the militia resumed.
